doc.title: James Chirillo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Finegan's story of Bartok, Palestrina and Eddie Sauter
summary: Finegan's account of Eddie Sauter asking Bartok for advice and being told to study Palestrina, and Bartok's choral pieces.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: know the tune, you’re going to play the tune. That’s it. It’s not like you’re going to rehearse it or anything. So how do you make those same notes sound fresh? And it’s the same thing with writing a great arrangement or if you write a piece, you write a tune, whatever it is, your ideas, how do you make them sound fresh but still logically a coherent part of the whole. And so yeah, of course, studying Brahms, oh man Brahms, Gabrieli, all those guys, Palestrina. Now this is something that Finegan told me now dig this. Eddie Sauter wrote for Benny Goodman. Benny Goodman hired Bartok, he commissioned, they played that “Contrasts.” He wrote that “Contrasts” for Joseph Szigeti himself to play on the piano and Benny Goodman on the clarinet, right? And Bartok came, and Szigeti, maybe he was already here, whatever. He came to New York and they recorded that at RCA in nineteen thirty whatever it was. Maybe it was early forties, I forget. But okay, so Eddie Sauter, I mean he knew Benny. I mean he made it a point of I’m going to get down to RCA that day, and so Bill Finegan told me this, at a quiet moment in the action Eddie Sauter went up to Béla Bartok and introduced himself and you know, “Maestro Bartok, I’m a writer myself” and on and what you’ve done. “What advice do you have for the young writer?” And he said the only thing Bartok would tell him was, “Study Palestrina.” Now dig that. And then now you get into Bartok a little more, as far as you start really checking into some of the things he’s done besides just like the really main pieces like “Concerto for Orchestra” or something like that, and you find that he’s written 27 two or three part vocal — pieces for vocal chorus, for either childrens’ or womens’ chorus, 27 small pieces. And these are a direct result of him studying a book on sixteenth century counterpoint in the style — by a Danish musicologist named Jeppesen, and Bartok read it, on dissonance in the style of Palestrina. Kodaly said he was always bugging Bartok, “Why don’t you write some vocal music already? Come on, we need some vocal.” He ended up reading that book and getting into Palestrina’s style like that and he wrote those 27 pieces. And to hear how he works and overlaps those motifs and everything, with some of those Hungarian scales and those Hungarian modes and his sense of rhythm and everything. It’s — oh man those things are beautiful. If you ever get a chance to hear those check those out.
